level_mis_links.exact_rule: wrong rule: a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations. Right rule: A variable declared inside the body is in scope only to the end of the body, so each pass declares and initializes it afresh and it does not keep the previous pass's value.

Applies the update rule (LT) unevenly: adds the new value to the previous total on some passes but restarts from the initial value (or forgets to add) on others. (here mixing in: "a variable declared in the loop body lives across all iterations")

wrong rule: The computer recognises that one variable plays two roles, e.g. input value and running total, and keeps the values apart; it knows which variable is the counter and which the sum. Right rule: A variable holds one value at a time; each role (input, counter, running total) needs its own variable and explicit update.

wrong rule: Values changed by one pass of a loop (other than the loop variable) do not affect later passes. Right rule: Each pass starts from the state left by the previous pass, so a change in one pass carries into the next ones.

Changing the initial value shifts the result by that amount (sum starts at 1 gives sum + 1); a product starting at 0 stays 0; reordering the items does not change an integer sum (addition is commutative) but may change a floating-point sum slightly.
wrong rule: a^2 computes a squared. Right rule: Java has no exponent operator; ^ is exclusive or, and a * a or Math.pow(a, 2) computes a squared.

Points to LT (evaluate operands, then apply the operator in the promoted type). Applied unevenly, a student uses integer division for one / and real division for another / in the same int expression. (here mixing in: "a^2 computes a squared")

wrong rule: "10" - 1 or "6" * "2" works because the strings look like numbers. Right rule: Arithmetic operators other than + are not defined for Strings; a String of digits must first be converted to a number, e.g. with Integer.parseInt.

Changing an operand's type changes the operator's meaning (int / versus double /). Reordering * and / changes integer results (59 * 100 / 60 is 98, 59 / 60 * 100 is 0). Replacing ^ with Math.pow gives a real power.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them.
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: a = b copies the value of a into b. Right rule: Assignment stores the value of the right side into the variable on the left.
wrong rule: a = b adds the value of b to the value already in a (the accumulator model). Right rule: a = b replaces the old value of a with the value of b; the old value is lost.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.
wrong rule: b = a exchanges the values of a and b. Right rule: b = a copies a into b and leaves a unchanged; an exchange needs a temporary variable and three assignments.
wrong rule: After b = a, a no longer holds a value, as if the value had been moved. Right rule: Assignment copies; the variable on the right keeps its value.

Points to LT (evaluate the right side with current values, then overwrite the left variable). Applied unevenly, a student traces one segment correctly but reads the next as simultaneous equations or as a swap, giving 15 and 15 for one segment and 5 and 10 for the other. (here mixing in: "= stores the expression itself, not its computed value")
wrong rule: a[i] = a[j]; a[j] = a[i]; exchanges the two values. Right rule: A temporary variable must save a[i] before it is overwritten.
wrong rule: assigning a reference copies the object. Right rule: b = a; copies only the reference, so a and b refer to the same array and b[i] = v also changes a[i].
wrong rule: A variable keeps its first value after a new assignment (the static model). Right rule: Each assignment or read replaces the variable's current value.

Swapping the two sides (a = b versus b = a) changes which variable changes. Reordering assignments changes the final values. An assignment cannot be undone, because the old value is lost unless it was first saved in a temporary.
wrong rule: You must write == true / == false to test a boolean. Right rule: if (b) already tests b, and if (!b) tests that it is false, so == true adds nothing.
wrong rule: You need an if to turn a boolean expression into a boolean. Right rule: ok = (x > y); stores the result of the comparison directly.
wrong rule: You need ? : to turn a boolean expression into a boolean (ok = x > y ? true : false). Right rule: ok = (x > y); already gives the boolean, so the ? : is unnecessary.
wrong rule: A true/false question is answered with arithmetic (e.g. 1 for true). Right rule: A logic question is written as a boolean expression whose value is true or false, e.g. (year % 4 == 0).

Points to LT (arithmetic first, then comparisons, then !, &&, ||, left to right, with short-circuit). Applied unevenly: the student evaluates && before a comparison in one sub-expression, or evaluates the right operand of && on a pass where the left was already false. (here mixing in: "you must write == true / == false to test a boolean")

wrong rule: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100. Right rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean, which cannot be compared with <); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

wrong rule: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once. Right rule: A test made once is an if; a while re-tests its condition and repeats its body for as long as the condition is true.

wrong rule: A condition on several values has to be written as nested if statements, one value per if. Right rule: Several conditions combine into one boolean expression with && and ||, e.g. if (x == 0 && y == 0).

Rewriting with De Morgan (!(a && b) as !a || !b) keeps the value for every input; swapping the operands of && keeps the truth value but can change whether the right operand is evaluated (and whether a guard still protects it); changing < to <= changes the result only at the boundary value.
wrong rule: 90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100. Right rule: a < b < c does not compile (a < b is a boolean); a range test is written 90 <= grade && grade <= 100.

wrong rule: == compares the contents of two Strings. Right rule: s == t is true only when s and t refer to the same object; "abc" == "ab" + x is false even when x is "c"; s.equals(t) compares the text.
wrong rule: s < t compares two Strings alphabetically. Right rule: < and > are defined only for primitive types; comparing Strings with them does not compile (use s.compareTo(t)).
wrong rule: < and > mean the same thing (or a < b means a is greater than b). Right rule: a < b is true when a is smaller than b; a > b when a is larger.

Points to LT (evaluate both operands, promote to a common type, then compare). Applied unevenly: the student treats < as <= on the boundary pass of a loop, or compares an int with a double as ints on one line and as doubles on another. (here mixing in: "90 <= grade <= 100 tests whether grade is between 90 and 100")
wrong rule: = compares two values instead of assigning. Right rule: x = y copies the value of y into x; x == y is what compares them and produces a boolean.
wrong rule: You must write == true / == false to test a boolean. Right rule: if (b) already tests b, so writing == true adds nothing.
wrong rule: .equals() compares references, not contents. Right rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters; it is == that compares references.

Changing < to <= (or > to >=) changes the result only at the boundary value, which in a loop guard means one more or one fewer iteration (off-by-one); mirroring the comparison (a < b to b > a) preserves the value; negating it gives the complementary operator (!(a < b) is a >= b).

wrong rule: x += 0.5 adds one half to an int x. Right rule: x += 0.5 means x = (int) (x + 0.5) for an int x, so the sum is cast back to int and truncated: x stays the same (x = 3 gives 3.5, cast to 3).
wrong rule: x[i] -= y sets x[i] to -y (reads -= as assignment of a negated value). Right rule: x[i] -= y means x[i] = x[i] - y: it subtracts y from the current value.

Applies the compound-assignment rule (LT) unevenly: uses the current value of x on some passes but treats x -= y as x = -y on others, or forgets the implicit cast on some lines. (here mixing in: "x += 0.5 adds one half to an int x")

For a variable of the same type as the result, replacing x op= e by x = x op e preserves behaviour; when x is narrower (int x, double e), x = x op e no longer compiles, so the two are not always interchangeable. Swapping += and -= reverses the effect of each pass.
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom.

wrong rule: The program knows or sees what later lines will do and acts on those goals at the current line, e.g. it stops 'at ten' because it wants to draw a box. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: e.g. runs a later line before an earlier one, lets an if that was already passed fire again later, or ends the program when a loop or a false if ends instead of continuing with the next statement. (here mixing in: "Statements in a program can run in any order")
wrong rule: When the then branch runs, the code after the if is skipped. Right rule: After the if finishes, execution continues with the next statement either way.
wrong rule: logical AND/OR always evaluate both sides (Java short-circuits them). Right rule: In p && q, q is evaluated only when p is true; in p || q, q is evaluated only when p is false.

wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.

wrong rule: An IF statement earlier in the program stays active and fires later, e.g. inside a later loop, when its condition becomes true. Right rule: An if is evaluated once when control reaches it; afterwards it is inactive unless control returns to it.

wrong rule: When an if condition is false (and there is no else), control jumps back to the start of the program. Right rule: A false condition skips the then branch and execution continues with the statement after the if statement.

wrong rule: An if statement watches its condition while the program runs and fires as soon as the condition becomes true (if = whenever). Right rule: An if condition is tested once, when control reaches the if statement; later changes to the variables do not trigger the branch.
wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

Reordering two statements generally changes the result whenever one reads a variable that the other writes (e.g. swapping x = x + 1 and print(x)); reordering is safe only for statements that touch disjoint variables. Moving a statement into or out of a branch or loop body changes how many times it runs (0, 1 or n).

wrong rule: Java recognises which variable is the counter and which is the running total, and keeps their values apart even if one variable is used for both. Right rule: A variable holds one value at a time and Java infers no roles: a counter needs its own variable, initialised before the loop (`int wins = 0;`) and updated only by its own statement (`wins++`).

wrong rule: int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned. Right rule: A declaration creates the variable (its storage) with its type; assignment later puts a value in it.

Points to LT (a declaration runs once when reached and creates the variable, and later assignments only update it). Applied unevenly, a student re-creates or zeroes the variable on some passes but not others, or treats a declaration further down as already in effect. (here mixing in: "int x; without a value sets aside no memory; the variable only exists once something is assigned")

wrong rule: A variable declared int can hold 2.5 or "hi"; the type is only a label. Right rule: A data type is a set of values and a set of operations defined on them, so an int variable holds only int values.
wrong rule: local variables get a default value on their own. Right rule: A local variable has no value until it is assigned, and using it before then does not compile.

Moving a declaration into an inner block (such as a loop body) shrinks its scope and re-creates the variable on each pass, so an accumulated value is lost. Moving it out widens its scope. Changing its type changes which values and operations are legal.

wrong rule: Dividing by zero always stops the program with an error. Right rule: Only integer division (and remainder) by zero throws; 1.0/0.0 is Infinity and 0.0/0.0 is NaN, and the program keeps running.
wrong rule: System.out.println(5 / 0); is rejected by the compiler. Right rule: It compiles; the ArithmeticException (/ by zero) is thrown when the program runs and reaches the division.

Points to LT (both operands are evaluated, promotion decides whether the division is int or double, and only then is the divisor checked). Applied unevenly: the student lets 1/0.0 crash because the 1 is an int, or lets 1/0 give Infinity on one line and an exception on another. (here mixing in: "Dividing by zero always stops the program with an error")

Changing an operand from int to double turns a crash into a silent Infinity or NaN (and changing it back turns the silent value into a crash); adding a zero guard leaves results for nonzero divisors unchanged.
wrong rule: a single literal or variable "isn't an expression". Right rule: A single variable or literal is an expression whose value is just that value.

Points to LT (replace each variable with its current value, then apply operators in precedence order). Applied unevenly, a student substitutes current values for some variables and old or future values for others, or respects precedence in one subexpression only. (here mixing in: "a single literal or variable "isn't an expression"")
wrong rule: an assignment cannot be used inside a larger expression. Right rule: An assignment is an expression whose value is the value assigned, so (x = v) both stores v in x and gives v.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.

wrong rule: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction. Right rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.
wrong rule: = stores the expression itself, not its computed value. Right rule: y = x + k; stores the value that x + k has at that moment, so later changes to x do not change y.
wrong rule: nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first. Right rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

wrong rule: An assignment states a lasting equality between its two sides, so y = x - y can be solved like the equation x = 2y and x = x + 5 relates two equal quantities. Right rule: An assignment is a one-time action: evaluate the right side with current values, then store the result in the left variable.

Adding parentheses that match the default grouping keeps the value, and rewriting with an equivalent formula (4 * (x - 3) as 4*x - 12) keeps it for ints. Changing one operand's type (3 to 3.0) can change both the result's type and its value.

wrong rule: The file a filter processes shows up in args[]. Right rule: A filter reads only standard input. The file or upstream program is attached by < or |, and args[] carries only parameters such as lo and hi.

Points to LT (read one value, test it, maybe print it, repeat). An uneven trace prints out-of-range values on some passes, or holds all the output until the end. (here mixing in: "a redirected file shows up in args[]")
A filter keeps the relative order of the values it passes (it outputs a subsequence). Filters can be chained in any number without changing each other.
wrong rule: x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x. Right rule: Both increment i, but ++i has the value after the increment and i++ the value before.
wrong rule: i++ increases i by 2. Right rule: i++ (and ++i) increases i by exactly 1.

Applies the increment rule (LT) unevenly: uses the old value in one expression and the new value in another for the same i++, or performs the increment at the end of the loop body instead of where it is written. (here mixing in: "x = i++ and x = ++i store the same value in x")
wrong rule: i = i++ increases i by 1. Right rule: i++ evaluates to the old value, so i = i++ stores the old value back.
wrong rule: ++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass. Right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.

wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.
As a stand-alone statement, replacing i++ by ++i, i += 1 or i = i + 1 preserves behaviour; inside an expression (x = i++ vs x = ++i) the swap changes the value used by 1.

wrong rule: The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction. Right rule: The type of a numerical expression is determined by the expression, so double d = a / b; with int a and b still divides as ints.
wrong rule: 10 / 3 evaluates to 3.333. Right rule: Dividing two ints gives an int: the fractional part is discarded.
wrong rule: Changing a later literal to 100.0 fixes an earlier int division. Right rule: The int division happens first; the double must be in the division itself.

Points to LT (each / looks at its own two operand types when it is evaluated). Applied unevenly, a student evaluates 9/5 as 1.8 in f = (9/5)*c + 32 but as 1 elsewhere, or assumes a later double operand rescues an earlier int division. (here mixing in: "The type of a numerical expression depends on the type expected by the surrounding context, so double d = a / b; keeps the fraction")

wrong rule: Making every variable a double is the right fix for integer division. Right rule: Use int for countable things and double for measured ones; where a fraction is needed, make one operand of the division a double (or cast) instead of changing every type.
wrong rule: (double) (3 / 5) is 0.6. Right rule: The integer division 3 / 5 = 0 happens before the cast, so the result is 0.0.
wrong rule: a % b is never negative, and integer division of a negative number rounds down. Right rule: a / b rounds toward 0 and a % b takes the sign of a: -14 / 3 is -4 and -14 % 3 is -2.

Making one operand a double (10.0 / 3) keeps the fraction (3.333...). Casting after the division does not. Multiplying before dividing preserves precision (59 * 100 / 60 is 98). Changing an operand's sign changes only the quotient's sign, since rounding is toward zero.
wrong rule: The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start. Right rule: A while or for body runs zero times when the condition is false at the start.

wrong rule: Some statements inside the braces of a loop body are not repeated; they run once, before or after the loop. Right rule: Every statement inside the loop braces is part of the body and runs on every pass.

wrong rule: A statement written after the loop is repeated with the loop body. Right rule: The body ends at the closing brace (or after its single statement); code after it runs once, after the loop ends.

wrong rule: A loop runs its first body statement all N times, then its second body statement all N times. Right rule: Each pass runs the whole body in order, so the body statements interleave: S1, S2, S1, S2, ...

wrong rule: Values changed by one pass of a loop (other than the loop variable) do not affect later passes. Right rule: Each pass starts from the state left by the previous pass, so a change in one pass carries into the next ones.

Applies the body rule (LT) unevenly: runs all body statements on some passes but only some on others, includes the statement after the loop on some passes, or uses stale values from the first pass later. (here mixing in: "The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start")

wrong rule: The loop stops the moment the condition becomes false, even in the middle of the body. Right rule: The condition is tested only before each pass, so the whole body finishes before the loop can stop.

wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command. Right rule: The computer executes only what the code states; every needed step and value must be written.

wrong rule: An if inside a loop body runs its branch on every pass without testing its condition. Right rule: The if condition is tested again on every pass, with the current values, so the branch runs only on passes where it is true.

wrong rule: The repeat count of a counted loop says how many of the body statements are executed. Right rule: The repeat count is how many times the whole body runs; every pass runs all body statements.

wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.

wrong rule: A loop prints the same thing on every pass; the changing loop variable does not affect what the body does. Right rule: The body uses the current value of the loop variable, so its output can differ on each pass.

Moving a statement from inside the body to after the loop changes it from running once per pass to once in total (and vice versa); reordering two body statements that share a variable changes the results (e.g. increment before vs after use).
wrong rule: ++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass. Right rule: The update runs after each pass of the body, so with either ++i or i++ the first pass uses i = s.
wrong rule: < vs <= and 0..n vs 0..n-1 are interchangeable. Right rule: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) runs n times with i going up to n - 1; with <= it runs n + 1 times and reaches i = n.

Applies the init-test-update rule (LT) unevenly: updates before the body on some passes, skips the test or the update on a pass, or re-runs the init. (here mixing in: "++i in the for-update runs before the body each pass")

wrong rule: a condition that never goes false still terminates. Right rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops.

wrong rule: for (double x = 0.0; x <= 1.0; x += 0.1) runs exactly 11 times. Right rule: Using a double as a for-loop index is legal but bad practice: the number of iterations depends on an equality test between double values, which may not give the result you expect.

wrong rule: An array loop processes the whole array from index 0 to length-1 and increments its index at the end of the body, whatever the code says. Right rule: The loop visits exactly the indices that its initialisation, guard and update produce, in the order in which its statements are written.

wrong rule: The initialization, condition and update of a for header are equations that all hold at the same time. Right rule: The three header parts are statements run at different moments: init once, then condition test, body, update, repeated.

wrong rule: A pass of a loop may leave out one of its parts (the condition test, the body, the update, or the initialization). Right rule: Each pass of a for loop runs test, then body, then update, every time; the initialization runs once, at the start.

wrong rule: The update part of a for header (e.g. i = i - 4) runs before the body on each pass, so the first pass already sees the updated value. Right rule: The update runs after the body, before the next condition test; the first pass uses the initial value.

wrong rule: The update of the loop variable can change from pass to pass (e.g. switch direction) although the code is the same. Right rule: The update expression is the same on every pass; the loop variable changes by the rule written in the update.

wrong rule: A loop variable always goes up or down by 1, whatever the update says (so i = i - 4 is read as i--). Right rule: The loop variable changes exactly as the update expression says (i += 2, i = i - 4, i *= 2, ...).

Changing < to <= adds one pass; starting at 1 instead of 0 removes one; doubling the step halves the passes; reversing init and bound with i-- visits the same values in reverse order (and still processes the same set only if both ends are adjusted).

wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println(); and a random number is Math.random().
wrong rule: Nested calls run outside-in, not arguments-first. Right rule: In f(g(x)), g(x) is evaluated first and its result is passed to f.

wrong rule: Java works out from the variable names which argument goes where, so Math.pow(n, 2) and Math.pow(2, n) mean the same. Right rule: Arguments are matched to parameters by position, in the order the signature lists them; Math.pow(a, b) raises a to the bth power.

wrong rule: A method call lists the parameter types, as in Math.pow(double a, double b). Right rule: A call passes only argument expressions, e.g. Math.pow(a, b); types appear only in the signature/declaration.

Points to LT (arguments are evaluated left to right, then the method runs, then its return value replaces the call). Applied unevenly: in f(g(x)) the student calls the outer method before the inner one on some lines, or keeps the argument expression unevaluated in one trace step. (here mixing in: "() are optional on a no-argument call like println")
wrong rule: You call length() instead of using the length field. Right rule: An array's size is the field a.length, written without parentheses (String has the method s.length()).
wrong rule: .equals() compares references, not contents. Right rule: s.equals(t) checks whether the two Strings contain the same characters.

Changing an argument changes only the returned value, never the argument variable; swapping arguments changes the meaning (Math.pow(2, n) vs Math.pow(n, 2)); replacing a call by its value keeps behaviour for mathematical functions but not for Math.random().
wrong rule: print and println behave the same. Right rule: println ends the line after printing and print does not, so print(s1); print(s2); puts s1 and s2 on the same line.
wrong rule: println(s) prints a newline and then s. Right rule: println(s) prints s and then the line terminator.

Applies the println rule (print, then end line) unevenly: puts the newline before the text on one call and after it on another, or forgets that the next output starts on a new line. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: System.out.Println and System.out.println name the same method. Right rule: Java is case-sensitive: names that differ only in capitalization are different names.
wrong rule: () are optional on a no-argument call like println. Right rule: A method call always needs parentheses, so an empty line is printed with System.out.println();.
Replacing println with print joins the next output onto the same line (a typical logic error); the characters printed stay the same.
wrong rule: Code that compiles is code that works. Right rule: Code that compiles can still fail at run time (an exception) or give wrong output.
wrong rule: System.out.println(5 / 0); is rejected by the compiler. Right rule: It compiles; integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException when the statement runs.

Applies the exception rule (LT: execution stops at the faulty statement) unevenly: lets the program keep printing after the failing statement on one trace, or reports the error before any earlier output on another. (here mixing in: "Code that compiles is code that works")
wrong rule: Integer.parseInt works on any text, e.g. "five" or "12.2". Right rule: Integer.parseInt throws a NumberFormatException at run time when the string is not an integer written in digits.

The same compiled program may run fine on one input and throw on another (UseArgument with and without an argument); adding a guard such as checking args.length removes the trigger without changing correct runs.

wrong rule: The sentinel value (e.g. 99999) is added to the total like the other values. Right rule: The value is tested against the sentinel before it is processed. The loop stops at the sentinel, which is never added or counted.

Points to LT (read, test for the sentinel, then process). An uneven trace processes before testing on the last pass, so the sentinel is included that time. (here mixing in: "The sentinel value (e.g. 999999) is added to the total like the other values")
Changing the sentinel keeps the behaviour only if the new value cannot occur in the data. Moving the test after the processing step breaks the invariant that the sentinel is never processed.
wrong rule: Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice. Right rule: Each read consumes its value, so the second call returns the next value.

wrong rule: Reading a second input value into a variable that already holds one is an error, so the program cannot run. Right rule: A later read assigns a new value, which overwrites the old one. y = StdIn.readInt(); y = StdIn.readInt(); is legal, and y keeps the second value.

Points to LT (each call blocks, then consumes exactly one token, in order). An uneven trace gives a variable a value that was already consumed, skips a token on some reads, or merges two READs into one. (here mixing in: "Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice")

wrong rule: A line read after a number read returns the next line typed. Right rule: readInt() stops right after the number and leaves the rest of that line, including the line separator. A following readLine() returns that rest (often ""), not the next line.

wrong rule: Reading a value once before the loop is enough; the loop will process each new input value. Right rule: A loop must call a read inside its body on every pass. A single read before the loop gives one value, which is processed over and over.

Changing the input data changes the results without recompiling. Swapping two reads swaps the values the two variables get. Changing readInt to readDouble accepts more inputs; the reverse breaks on tokens like 12.2.
wrong rule: print and println behave the same (no newline difference). Right rule: println(s) prints s and then ends the line, but print(s) does not, so print("a"); print("b"); gives ab on one line.

Points to LT (output appears in the order the output calls execute, with a line break only after println). An uneven trace drops a repeated value, puts output lines out of order, or adds line breaks after print on some calls. (here mixing in: "print and println behave the same (no newline difference)")
wrong rule: printf() ends the line like println(). Right rule: printf() adds no newline. Put \n (or %n) in the format string to end the line.

wrong rule: An output statement that names the same variable twice (WRITE y, x, y) prints it only once. Right rule: Every expression in the output is printed, so System.out.println(y + " " + x + " " + y) with x=6, y=9 prints 9 6 9.
Switching System.out.print/println to StdOut.print/println keeps the output. Changing println to print keeps every character but removes the line break, so lines join.
wrong rule: The computer fills in omitted steps or values the programmer meant. Right rule: The computer executes only the statements written; every needed step and value must be written.

Applies the sequencing rule (LT) unevenly: executes the statements in order on some lines but lets a later statement's effect leak into an earlier one, or skips or repeats a statement on one pass. (here mixing in: "The computer fills in omitted steps or values that the programmer meant, e.g. REPEAT 4 [FORWARD 30] draws a square without a turn command")
wrong rule: Statements in a program can run in any order, so their order makes no difference. Right rule: Without control statements, statements run once each, top to bottom, in the order written.

wrong rule: Line breaks and indentation change what the program does, so each statement must be on its own line. Right rule: Java compilers treat all whitespace outside quotes as equivalent; statements are separated by ;, not by line breaks.

wrong rule: The program knows what later lines will do and acts on that goal at the current line. Right rule: Each statement executes using only the current state; later lines have no effect until control reaches them.
Swapping two statements that touch the same variable or the output generally changes the result; swapping independent statements, or changing only whitespace between them, keeps it.

wrong rule: Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice. Right rule: Each read consumes the value it returns, so a second StdIn.readInt() returns the next value in the stream (input 3 5 gives 3, then 5).

Points to LT (reads take values from the front in order; prints append at the end in order). An uneven trace reuses an already-consumed value on some reads, or writes some output out of execution order. (here mixing in: "Calling StdIn.readInt() twice returns the same value twice")
Changing where a stream comes from or goes to (keyboard, file, pipe, another device) keeps the program's behaviour. Changing the order of two reads swaps which value lands in which variable.
wrong rule: For and while loops end when the condition becomes true. Right rule: A for or while loop ends when its condition becomes false.

wrong rule: The loop stops the moment the condition becomes false, even in the middle of the body. Right rule: The condition is tested only before each pass, so the whole body finishes before the loop can stop.
wrong rule: Uses a loop where a condition needs to be tested only once. Right rule: A test made once is an if; a loop repeats.

wrong rule: Testing one case is enough; Java will repeat the test for the other values by itself. Right rule: A statement runs once each time control reaches it; repeating a test for many values needs a loop.
wrong rule: When a loop finishes the program ends, so code after the loop never runs. Right rule: When the loop condition becomes false, control continues with the first statement after the loop.

wrong rule: How many times a loop runs is decided by what the program is meant to do, so it may go on after its condition is false. Right rule: The loop runs only while its condition is true when tested; it stops at the first false test.

wrong rule: If a loop condition is false at first but would become true later, the loop still runs (it repeats or skips until the condition is true, then runs until it is false). Right rule: A while loop whose condition is false at the first test runs zero times; nothing later revives it.

wrong rule: A task that must be repeated is written once, without a loop, as if one pass were enough. Right rule: A step that must happen several times (or an unknown number of times) needs a loop such as while or for; code without a loop runs once.

Applies the while rule (LT) unevenly: tests the condition before some passes but not others, stops in the middle of a body on one pass, or runs the first pass without testing. (here mixing in: "For and while loops end when the condition becomes true")
wrong rule: an if body repeats while its condition holds. Right rule: An if body runs at most once; only a loop repeats its body.
wrong rule: The loop body always runs at least once, even if the condition is false at the start. Right rule: A while or for body runs zero times when the condition is false at the start.

wrong rule: a condition that never goes false still terminates. Right rule: A while loop stops only when its condition is false at a check, so if no pass changes the variables in the condition, it never stops.
wrong rule: If my loop never ends, the compiler or Java will warn me. Right rule: Java cannot detect infinite loops in general; you must check that the loop condition eventually becomes false.
wrong rule: Some loops can only be written with for, others only with while. Right rule: Any for loop can be rewritten as a while loop and vice versa; for just packages init, test and update.

wrong rule: A loop is an iterative if-else: while the condition is true the body repeats, and when it is false the code after the loop repeats. Right rule: Only the body is repeated; once the condition is false the code after the loop runs once.

wrong rule: A while loop ends by itself even if nothing in the body changes the variable tested in the condition. Right rule: If no statement in the body changes a variable in the condition, a condition that was true stays true and the loop never ends.

Changing < to <= adds exactly one pass at the boundary; removing the update from the body makes a loop that was entered never end; a condition that is false initially gives zero passes whatever the body does. Rewriting as for (init; cond; update) preserves behaviour if no continue is involved.
